claims.text: Dash's blockchain is a public ledger: an ordered, timestamped record of transactions designed to protect against double spending and modification of earlier transaction records.
Transactions are collected into blocks, and each block header contains a commitment to that block's transactions plus the hash of the preceding block's header.

The accepted historical record is append-only: the chain advances by adding a block, while changing an accepted transaction would also require changing its block and every following block. A correction therefore belongs in a later entry rather than overwriting the original entry.
In the baseline proof-of-work model, hash linkage makes tampering evident, but hashing alone does not make constructing a competing history economically expensive. Proof of work supplies that cost.

Dash full nodes independently validate blocks against shared consensus rules before accepting and relaying them; archival nodes retain the entire chain, while pruned full nodes may retain only part of the historical block data.

Changing one operator's local copy does not rewrite the network's accepted record. Dash full nodes independently reject blocks that fail their rules; accumulated work is part of the baseline chain-selection model, not a complete statement of current Dash acceptance.

In the baseline proof-of-work model, a party constructing a competing history must redo the proof of work for the changed block and its descendants while honest participants continue extending the original chain. The required work grows as more blocks follow the target block.

Proof of work makes constructing a competing historical chain expensive rather than mathematically impossible. Current Dash has additional acceptance rules that reject some competing blocks regardless of accumulated work, so a more-work chain is not guaranteed to become accepted history.
Without a central repository or authority, participants can share and independently check a record without trusting the application operator to preserve the sole authoritative copy.

A builder gives up unilateral administration in exchange for that independence: accepted history cannot be silently patched or deleted, and changing shared validation rules requires network participants to adopt compatible rules or risk divergent chains.

A Git commit history is a useful structural analogy because commits point backward and later identifiers depend on earlier history. Its limit teaches the main distinction: a repository owner can force-push, whereas independently validating blockchain full nodes do not accept one operator's rewritten copy merely because that operator published it.

uncertainties.topic: Should append-only be described as every node permanently storing every historical byte?
uncertainties.resolution: Define append-only at the ledger level: accepted records are not overwritten, and corrections arrive as later entries. Do not claim every node is archival.

uncertainties.topic: Should the lesson call blockchain history immutable?
uncertainties.resolution: Use tamper evident and costly to rewrite because immutable can imply that revision is impossible.

uncertainties.topic: Which familiar developer structure should carry the explanation?
uncertainties.resolution: Use Git commit history for the block-linking shape and an administrator-controlled database for the builder tradeoff. State that a repository owner can force-push, while one blockchain operator cannot impose a rewritten copy on independently validating nodes.
